national.title: Sullivan claims Peltola is 'still lying' about campaign's involvement in Alaska ballot controversy
national.summary: "There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," Sullivan told CNN's "State of the Union," two days before Election Day. "She got caught lying, and she's still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us."
national.body:
Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said Sunday that he doubted claims by his Democratic opponent that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting a retired schoolteacher also named Dan Sullivan onto the ballot to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the Senate.

Republicans have long suspected that Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, and her campaign were behind the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot. They say their suspicions were confirmed by a New York Times report last week that was based on interviews with Peltola's ex-campaign manager, text messages and campaign finance documents showing that an operative trying to recruit decoy candidates was paid by a group backing Peltola.

"There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," Sullivan told CNN's "State of the Union," two days before Election Day. "She got caught lying, and she's still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us."

Peltola has insisted she had nothing to do with recruiting the other Sullivan and has called the attention on it a "distraction" from the main issues facing Alaskans of high prices caused by the war in Iran launched by Republican Donald Trump. Her campaign has also denied involvement, as has the national Democratic operation that focuses on Senate races, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Before a rally Friday, Peltola was asked if it was possible someone on her campaign was involved in recruiting the other candidate: "I have no idea," she told KTUU. "I honestly have no idea."

The second Sullivan, who is listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. while the senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan and marked as a Republican incumbent, has long insisted he ran on his own accord.

Trump, who ordered his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit to stop certification of a possible Peltola win, called for the Democratic candidate to be prosecuted after the Times story was published. Federal agents descended on Alaska and issued subpoenas in the case, even though Republicans, including ones working with Trump, also have a long history of backing decoy candidates in elections. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.

national.title: Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui, Sweden's Andreas Almgren win 2026 NYC Marathon
national.summary: Tens of thousands of runners are participating in the 2026 TCS New York City marathon.
national.body: Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui won her second 2026 TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday, finishing the women's division in 2:24:35. Sweden's Andreas Almgren won the men's division in his marathon debut.Tens of thousands of runners from around the world take part in the iconic race through all five New York City boroughs, starting in Staten Island and finishing in Manhattan's Central Park. The 26.2-mile course is lined with crowds who flock annually to watch loved ones and strangers alike compete. Participants run the race in waves. On Sunday, the men's and women's professional wheelchair division kicked off the marathon from its starting point in Fort Wadsworth at around 8 a.m. ET, followed by hancyclists and select athletes with disabilities, and then the professional women's and men's open divisions. After that, five separate waves of runners started the marathon at different times between around 9 and 11:30 a.m.Kenyan long-distance stars Hellen Obiri and Benson Kipruto returned to the New York City Marathon this year as its defending champions, after Obiri won the women's open division and Kipruto won the men's division in 2025. Almgren, the World Half Marathon champion, joined them in his highly anticipated full marathon debut, as did Conner Mantz, the American marathon record-holder, who earned that title after completing the Chicago Marathon in 2 hours, 4 minutes and 43 seconds last year.NYC Marathon live tracker and resultsSpectators can get real-time updates on runners' progress with the New York Road Runners' interactive tracker here. Once the race is over, you'll find the winners and full results posted here.Map shows the 2026 NYC Marathon routeThe marathon route goes through all five boroughs, starting in Staten Island, across the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, then Queens, Manhattan and the Bronx before looping back down through Manhattan to the finish line in Central Park. national.title: FBI says North Korea was behind $6.3 billion Binance heist, the biggest crypto hack in history
national.summary: The bureau said in a statement that the attack was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
national.body:
Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.

The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and "instant swap services."

Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved.

"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it," Trump said of the case. "We don't know if it's North Korea." Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.

national.title: Shapiro says officials must "lead by example" in heated rhetoric
national.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said that officials must "lead by example" amid what he called "dangerous" campaign rhetoric that's escalated as Election Day approaches.
national.body: Washington — Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said Sunday that lawmakers must "lead by example" amid what he called "dangerous" campaign rhetoric that's escalated as Election Day approaches."I think what you do is try and lead by example — as we are trying to do here, as I am trying to do here — try and bring back kindness in the face of the cruelty that we see from this president," Shapiro said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."Shapiro, who was first elected governor in 2022 and is seeking reelection this year, spoke about the threats against him and his family. He highlighted the arson attack on the governor's residence in 2025 after he and his family celebrated the Jewish holiday of Passover with a Seder in the residence, saying, "It weighs on me, but it doesn't control me." He said he has "profound differences from the person I'm running against, from the president and others.""But I don't think engaging in cruelty is the answer," Shapiro added. "I think it makes everyone less safe."Asked about the rhetoric on the campaign trail in places like Michigan, where a key Senate race is playing out, Shapiro said, "It's dangerous. It's hateful."Shapiro said that since the attack on the governor's mansion, "even more people have threatened me and my wife, our family — threatened us based on how I worship."While he said "it weighs on you, certainly, to know that there are people out there trying to do you harm," he said, "I would also tell you, it motivates me to keep doing what I do to not let the bad guys win." Shapiro said he and his family met before he opted to seek reelection, and "everybody agreed — can't let the bad guys win." "We've got to keep going forward," he said. "You got to stand up against the hate. You got to lead by example, and you got to try and bring some decency back to this country."

national.title: A new Georgia O'Keeffe exhibit opens a window to unfamiliar works
national.summary: An exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts, "Georgia O'Keeffe: Architecture," is painting a different portrait of the artist, best known for her depictions of flowers and desert landscapes.
national.body: When you hear the name Georgia O'Keeffe, architecture may not immediately come to mind. "So many people know Georgia O'Keeffe as a painter of flowers, or maybe they know her landscapes, or her paintings of bones; so, something like a barn, I know, is a surprise for many people," said curator Ben Colman. "Curiously, flower pictures represent only about 10% of her artwork."A new exhibit at the Detroit Institute of Arts, titled "Georgia O'Keeffe: Architecture," is painting a different portrait of the artist, showcasing her architectural works through an autobiographical lens. "We are looking at the places where she lived and worked, the places that were really formative to her as an individual and as a painter," said Colman.O'Keeffe was born in 1887 on a Wisconsin dairy farm, a source of inspiration in her works. "When she painted ["My Shanty, Lake George"], she wanted to challenge what she considered misunderstandings of her art," said Colman. "She was very conscious, and maybe self-conscious, about selecting subjects that would not be perceived as typically feminine in their composition."She would later live in Manhattan, just as skyscrapers began to redefine the city in the 1920s."She pays special attention to what she called the sky shapes, the negative space of sky, moon, and clouds that she saw around the buildings," Colman said. O'Keeffe eventually moved to New Mexico, where she found herself surrounded by adobe structures and desert landscapes.Over the course of her career, O'Keeffe would go on to complete about 140 architectural paintings. Colman said, "These are pictures where she's asking questions about the nature of the places where she lived, about the qualities of light, atmosphere, and texture of the buildings that she painted."Georgia O'Keeffe died in 1986 at 98 years old, her legacy grounded in a vast body of work, cementing her presence in American art. national.title: ICE agent charged with assault for hitting fleeing man with car in Houston will turn himself in, attorney says
national.summary: Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot.
national.body:
A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney.

Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air."

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday.

Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Teare played footage from Morales' body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming.

"I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives.

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales "threw the car" at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report.

national.title: How movie star James Stewart became a war hero
national.summary: In 1941 the Oscar-winning actor answered his nation's call, serving as a pilot in the Army Air Corps, and came home from WWII a changed man. The film "Jimmy" depicts his decision to enlist, and his emotional post-war return to the screen in "It's a Wonderful Life."
national.body: It's trite but true; Jimmy Stewart played the Everyman better than everyone. He had the gawky innocence to be an idealistic senator, in "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington"; an eccentric with a six-foot-tall rabbit pal in "Harvey"; and a depth, in "Rear Window" and "Vertigo," that even Alfred Hitchcock found mysterious.But it was director Frank Capra who gave us the Jimmy Stewart that everyone still depends on every Christmas. "It's a Wonderful Life" is remarkable for a lot of reasons, not the least of which is that Stewart's memorable performance was his first after an almost-five-year absence from Hollywood. Audiences hadn't seen him on screen since 1941, the same year he took home the Academy Award for "The Philadelphia Story." He was a Hollywood A-lister. But not long after, he found himself on another list: the list for the draft. Stewart could have served safely stateside doing recruiting films and such. But he wanted, or at least felt, he needed to do more. Already an accomplished pilot, Stewart enlisted in the Army Air Corps. "He knew that America needed good pilots; he was one," said Janie McKirgan, curator at the Jimmy Stewart Museum in his hometown of Indiana, Pennsylvania. McKirgan said few wanted to let Hollywood's golden boy actually fly: "It took a long time for him to find somebody in the Army Air Corps that was willing to take that risk," she said. "Because if Jimmy Stewart, Academy Award-winning Jimmy Stewart, got shot down, it would be a huge blow to troop morale, to America, to everything."His fight to be able to fight despite his celebrity is the subject of a new film out this week, called "Jimmy." It stars Max Casella as director Frank Capra, and K.J. Apa as Jimmy Stewart. "We really set out to make the movie that Frank and Jimmy never got to make," Apa said. Casella said he was only vaguely aware of Stewart's wartime service; Apa did not know about it: "I can't believe it was true," he said. "It was the courage that made me dumbfounded of his story."Casella said, "He gave up Hollywood at the very top of the mountain." national.title: Shooting after Alabama football game leaves 1 dead, 8 injured
national.summary: The shooting outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, was among several violent incidents nationwide on Halloween weekend.
national.body: A mass shooting outside a football game in Alabama on Saturday killed one person and injured eight others, police said.The shooting happened outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual "Magic City Classic" football game. Police Chief Michael Pickett said most spectators and families had already left the stadium property when shots rang out. The shooting, he said, happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.Pickett said it was a "completely senseless act of violence" and that he was "very grateful that more people weren't injured.""This is something that we not only just see here in Birmingham, but we see it all over the nation," he said. "And it's important that we, as a community, address this issue."The circumstances of the shooting were unclear.Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and "multiple weapons" had been found and secured.Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday's game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.The Magic City Classic has such a deep history that Alabama State coach Eddie Robinson Jr., a former NFL linebacker and alumnus of the school, proposed creating a Hall of Fame for the game.The shooting in Alabama was among several violent incidents nationwide on Halloween weekend.In Dallas, three shootings unfolded within minutes of each other, leaving four people dead and five others with injuries in the downtown Deep Ellum neighborhood, CBS News Texas reported.And in Newark, Delaware, six people were shot shortly after 11:10 p.m. Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D'Elia said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city's Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting.

national.title: The legacy of Milwaukee's Socialist mayors
national.summary: Beginning in 1910, a city long associated with beer and bratwurst elected three Socialist mayors who made parks, public housing and sanitation priorities of city government, the benefits of which are still recognized in Milwaukee today.
national.body: Public servants going into government to clean things up? Sounds cliché! But at the Jones Island Water Reclamation Facility in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, that's job number one (and number two).As our guide Bill Graffin explains, this 101-year-old pioneering feat of engineering treats as much as 400 million gallons of wastewater each day.So, before the treatment center was built, how was water in Milwaukee treated? "It wasn't," Graffin replied.Kevin Shafer, executive director of Milwaukee's sewer system, explained: "All the sewage in the region went right to the rivers, which then went to Lake Michigan. And then we took our drinking water out of Lake Michigan."He said private industry could have built the sewage treatment system, "but that initial capital investment was huge. So, it really took a public tax base to pay for it."And that's just what happened in 1925 under the leadership of Milwaukee's Socialist mayor. In fact, Milwaukee was once the capital of American Socialism, and was the only major American city to elect three Socialist mayors. They collectively presided for nearly 40 years, beginning in 1910. So why, in Milwaukee of all places, did voters elect a Socialist government? "Because they were the best choice, absolutely," said John Gurda, the preeminent historian of Milwaukee. "You have a lot of things going on. One was corruption in high places, so there was an appetite for change; and then you had a huge working-class population as well – 57% of Milwaukee's males worked in manufacturing. 'Machine shop of world,' that was the self-signed slogan. So, appeals to that class consciousness were really well-received."Also key: the city's vibrant community of educated German immigrants who'd been raised with Socialist ideals before coming to America. They'd gather at Turner Hall. "This was really a center of German social life, as well as kind of an intellectual salon," said Gurda. "You got lectures here, lots of discourses, debates."Now, this was a distinctly practical, Midwestern flavor of Socialism, focused less on class warfare and more on what they said was improving the lives of working-class people: more parks, public housing, and functioning sewers, which is why it was dubbed "Sewer Socialism.""It was probably more social democracy back in those years," said Gurda, "and I think probably less ideological than practical."Asked if that was why it was

national.body: This year's midterm elections in Texas are on track to cost a billion dollars, with more than half of it spent on the U.S. Senate campaign – what could be the most expensive non-presidential race in American history. But whatever the price tag, it's certainly one of the most combative.Republican State Attorney General Ken Paxton's campaign bus displays a rally cry from the 19th century Texas revolution against Mexico: "Come and take it." Paxton, whose government tenure has been marked by controversy, is President Trump's hand-picked candidate. At a rally October 23, Paxton exhorted the crowd: "Do you believe in protecting Texas and stopping Sharia law? So do I. Do you believe that parents, not the government, should raise your children? So do I." Paxton's opponent is a Presbyterian seminarian and former middle-school teacher, State Representative James Talarico. Going into Election Day, polls show the two locked in a tight race.Talarico draws his campaign's closing theme from the TV show about Texas high-school football, "Friday Night Lights." He told a crowd in San Antonio Oct. 24, "To win this election, we have to execute. We have to leave it all on the field. We have to win."The issues in Texas mirror concerns across the country: high prices, immigration, government corruption, and the power of big tech and billionaires. As the song goes, "The eyes of Texas are upon you." And now, all eyes are on Texas. national.summary: Seven decades after the first reported sightings of Unidentified Flying Objects, a scientific council is investigating records and video released by the government of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), to possibly answer the question: Are we alone?
national.body: On a May evening back in 1950, Evelyn Trent had just finished feeding her rabbits when, she claims, she looked up and saw a slow-moving, metallic disk-shaped object hovering above her farm. Though some dismissed it as a hoax, her account was added to a growing list of unexplained events that sparked America's first UFO craze.At the annual McMenamins UFO Festival in McMinnville, Ore., just a few miles from Evelyn Trent's farm, there are costumes, a parade, and some theories that might be generously described as fringe: "Well, based on what I've read, it could be us from the future visiting us from, you know, the past," said one attendee, "and then it could also be trans-dimensional or inter-dimensional beings." Fringe, but definitely something Americans seem interested in. According to a CBS News Poll, nearly one in five Americans (17%) has seen a UFO, which has led to an explosion in podcasts and documentaries on the topic.Matthew Szydagis, one of the UFO festival's invited speakers, teaches physics at the State University of New York at Albany. He spoke to us about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (or UAPs), or what we used to call UFOs back in the old days: "I think the possibility that at least some small fraction of UFOs or UAPs represent a non-human intelligence," Szydagis said. "That will be the greatest discovery in human history. So, of course that's going to fire people up and get their imaginations going."Szydagis would like to believe in aliens, but he also knows that extraordinary claims demand extraordinary evidence, especially in the world of "UFOlogy," where the more extreme the claims, the more attention they get. national.summary: With elections to choose all 435 House members, a third of our Senators, and 36 governors, "Sunday Morning" looks at why – with rising costs and a historically unpopular president – this year's midterms may upend expectations.
national.body: Every four years, we get to choose our own president. But every two years, we have other elections, where we choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives, and a third of our Senators, and a whole lot of governors.This is a midterm elections year, our chance to steer the direction of the country."These are historically viewed as referenda on the job performance of a president," said New Yorker politics columnist Susan Glasser. She believes Tuesday's elections will be historic in a long list of ways.First, there's the matter of the president's steadily sinking popularity. "The president is the most unpopular American president in the history of modern polling going into a midterm election," Glasser said. The main reason is the price of everything. "People are so angry," Glasser said. "It's symbolized in how much money they're paying to put gas in their cars at the pump, or how much money they're paying for groceries. But it's obviously much, much broader than that."Another historic factor: The number of political ads. "This will be a record-breaking year basically any way you slice it," said Wesleyan University professor Erika Franklin Fowler, who studies political ads. "The amount of money that's being spent is enormous."This year, midterm ad spending will be over $11 billion, a record. But do political ads actually change anybody's mind? "Really not all that much," Fowler said. "No amount of advertising is going to change citizens' minds about the cost of goods in this type of economy."Also historic is the rise of artificial intelligence in the ads: Computer-generated scenes of candidates that look like real video. national.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
national.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
national.body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.

The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

national.title: It's ACA open enrollment time. Here are the changes for health insurance shoppers
national.summary: The ACA health insurance marketplaces — find yours at HealthCare.gov — open Nov. 1 for 2027 coverage. Getting an early start may be especially important this year.
national.body:
Christine Meehan, a hair stylist in Upper Chichester, Pa., has purchased health insurance through Pennie , the ACA marketplace for Pennsylvania. She's pictured here in October 2025. ACA open enrollment runs from Nov. 1 through Jan. 15 in most states. Tassanee Vejpongsa/AP hide caption

Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.

Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states . Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts started earlier, and some states have been allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.

A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.

Health Policy After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage .

One of the biggest changes for people shopping for their 2027 coverage will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents. The requirements are aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.

The new rules , outlined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.

For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.

national.title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
national.summary: The protests in cities across Germany - including Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt - came on the same day hundreds of thousands also protested in France.
national.body:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.

The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.

On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.

Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.

Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.

Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".

national.title: How Gen Z Republicans running for Congress are thinking about the future of the party
national.summary: On the eve of what may prove to be a tough election for the GOP, young conservatives vying to be part of the first class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress want a role shaping the party's next chapter.
national.body:
In northeast Iowa, 29-year-old Joe Mitchell is vying to represent the state's second congressional district. It's a competitive race, one of just a handful considered to be a tossup , as voters sour on President Trump and Democrats see control of Congress as increasingly in reach.

Mitchell has the president's endorsement, and if he's successful, he would head to Washington D.C. next year as part of a new cohort: the first-ever class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress.

It wouldn't be a large class. Aside from Mitchell, just a handful of other Gen Z Republicans are in the running for House seats this fall. One is running in a reliably red district. The rest are longshots, vying for what's seen as safe blue seats.

While their numbers may be small, Mitchell says the idea of a new generation of leaders in Washington is something that voters have been responding to on the campaign trail.

"I think people are looking for hope, regardless of what party they're in," he said. "They want to see young people get involved, and I hear that everywhere we go."

Only on NPR Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms The former state senator and real estate developer says his platform can speak to Iowans on both sides of the aisle. He's calling for term limits in the House, with a maximum of six terms, as well as a ban on congressional stock trading. He says he has also rejected campaign donations from corporate PACs.

It's all part of an "anti-corruption platform," a focus he says is uniquely rooted in his generation, as Americans under 30 report high levels of concern for their economic wellbeing and distrust of institutions.

"I just think that young people — on both sides of the aisle or no party affiliates — are frustrated with the system," he said. "They're frustrated and they should be."

national.summary: As polls close on election night, here's a look at what to expect each hour and which midterm races are key to deciding control of Congress.
national.body:
People grab stickers on the first day of early voting in New York, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Heather Khalifa/AP hide caption

Vote counting will start Tuesday night but could go on for days or even weeks.

While control of the House could become clear sooner because of bigger margins, control of the Senate could take much longer — the margins are tighter, seven states are especially competitive and two states use ranked choice voting which can prolong count time. Control of the House likely won't come down to one seat, but control of the Senate very well could.

As results are being tallied, here is a guide to watch election night as polls close across the country (all times in Eastern Time and organized by latest poll close time).

To jump to a specific poll closing time, use the links below: 7 p.m. ET | 7:30 p.m. ET | 8 p.m. ET | 8:30 p.m. ET | 9 p.m. ET | 10 p.m. ET | 11 p.m. ET | 12 a.m. ET | 1 a.m. ET

To get things started, all eyes are on the senate and gubernatorial races in Georgia and Florida.

Mike Collins in the race for Senate. The governor's race is tighter, one of the most competitive in the south between Republican nominee, billionaire businessman Rick Jackson and Democratic candidate, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Despite delays in elections past, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has told local news that new laws require counties to report results within an hour of polls closing.

South Carolina: This is an unexpectedly tight Senate race between Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after her brother Linsdey Graham died, and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Many national polls say the race in this heavily Republican state is a toss up, while the Cook Political Report says Republicans have the advantage.

national.title: Trump thanks supporters for the memories in final campaign stops for 2026 midterms
national.summary: President Trump has maintained a near-daily rally schedule as Election Day draws closer, playing his greatest hits for loyal crowds in red states in what is a sort-of goodbye to campaigning.
national.body:
President Trump was comparing his 2016 campaign rally size to the rallies Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders was having that year, when the president took a detour.

"We have the biggest rallies ever in history," Trump said, turning from braggadocious to reflective. "I hope you enjoy it because you're never going to see it again. You will never see what we've done. You'll never see it happen again."

Trump was in South Carolina to boost two Senate candidates who he personally picked but who have struggled to ignite excitement among Republican voters: Darline Graham in South Carolina and Michael Whatley in North Carolina.

This was one of Trump's final rallies after a flurry of midterm campaign events over the past month. More than 25 rallies in October alone, mostly in red states where Republicans are facing serious political headwinds. The official purpose is to help those Republicans win their races, but for a president whose trademark has always been big raucous rallies, there was more to it.

Trump won't be on the ballot again and once these midterms are over, it's not clear how many Republican candidates will want voters pretending he is. Right now, though, that is his plea.

"Please pretend I'm on the ballot cause in a way I am on the ballot, because they want to do away with all of the tremendous things we've done. The tax cuts, the border," Trump said last week at a rally in Greenville, N.C.

Like any performer on what could be a farewell tour, Trump plays a lot of the greatest hits. He has a regular riff about tariffs.

"Tariffs. The tariffs. My favorite word," Trump said in Lubbock, Tex. "I always say it, but I had to change it to fifth favorite. You've heard me say this. I said it's my favorite word. It's made us rich."

local.title: Donations keep Centaur Stride’s mission possible
local.summary: When everyone assumes somebody else will take responsibility, sometimes nobody does. There is an anonymous saying that captures this tendency to pass responsibility along: “This is a story about four people named Everybody, Somebody, Anybody, and Nobody. There was an important job to do, and Everybo
local.body:
Many facets of volunteering are pictured that include helping at events and fundraisers, art projects and helping get horses ready for riders.

When everyone assumes somebody else will take responsibility, sometimes nobody does.

There is an anonymous saying that captures this tendency to pass responsibility along: "This is a story about four people named Everybody, Somebody, Anybody, and Nobody. There was an important job to do, and Everybody was asked to do it. Everybody was sure Somebody would do it. Anybody could have done it, but Nobody did it. Somebody got angry because it was Everybody's job."

I have thought about those four people many times over the years. Lately, I have been thinking about them a lot.

When I visited my mother, I often helped her clean her house. One day, while clearing off her desk, I found three opened letters requesting donations. On each one, she had carefully recorded the check number, date, and amount she had contributed. Two were for monthly donations.

I asked her why she sent $30 every month to Save the Children. She explained that her contribution helped feed a child.

She understood something I needed to be reminded of: You don’t have to solve an entire problem to make a difference.

I work incredibly hard to raise the funds needed to keep Centaur Stride going. Many generous people help us, and I am deeply grateful for every one of them. But my mother was right about one thing: I had never directly asked her to contribute.

local.title: Behavior always part of equation with children
local.summary: It’s not often that I will refer to another writer’s thinking and observation of human behaviors in print. I am going to make an exception in this case. Mark Talley of Buffalo describes, in detail, his thinking about some of today’s youth. His mother, Geraldine Talley, was one of 10 people shot to d
local.body:
It’s not often that I will refer to another writer's thinking and observation of human behaviors in print. I am going to make an exception in this case. Mark Talley of Buffalo describes, in detail, his thinking about some of today's youth. His mother, Geraldine Talley, was one of 10 people shot to death by a white supremacist on May 14, 2022. He is also the author of "5/14 – the Day the Devil Came to Buffalo."

“My friends who are teachers see it every day. My other friends who are child psychologists who work at the office of Children and Family Services tell me that we are raising many children with no discipline, no accountability, no structure, and no responsibility. These thinking patterns are showing up in the work force and they are now impossible to ignore. We are raising a generation of kids that are not hire-able. A generation of "Mommy and Daddy kids" who say, "Please hold my hand" and who shut down the second life stops catering to them. In this day and age, and in this economy, that's a recipe for disaster. When we observe their lifestyle, factors such as no sleep, junk food, chemicals in everything we drink and eat, along with non-step stress. These factors hit motivation, confidence and behaviors. …

“Kids raised with all love and no limits appear to grow up with little resilience and no stress tolerance. They can talk about their feelings all day, but have great difficulty regulating them. Buffalo employers are observing it constantly – young adults who crumble under criticism, shut down when things get difficult and act like conflict is violence. Gentle parenting does not prevent trauma. It delays it. …

“Gentle parenting does not prepare Buffalo's young boys and girls for adulthood. It sets them up for collapse. We need to get back to parenting that mixes empathy with expectations, comfort with challenges, love with limits, or we are going to observe a generation who struggles under the weight of a world they were never taught to carry. Buffalo doesn't need harsher parents, just stronger ones.”

Mark has worked with many, many children in his lifetime. As you can read into his remarks, he obviously had a great mother that taught him values and not to ever quit and give up. He happens to be an African-American man in the inner city of Buffalo.

To think these problems are just inner-city problems is absurd. Many of you know me in this city as a teacher and basketball coach for more than 30 years. I apologize for nothing that I ever did when working with children, because I wasn't just teaching how to read or learn basketball, but taking these things into the future. Like Mark says, "When life hits you hard."

local.title: U.S. no longer keeps an open mind with elections
local.summary: This is the last weekend before the 2026 midterm elections. Most people have made up their minds already. Nevertheless, I’ll use this platform to express a few opinions about some recent controversies in an effort to urge people to think critically — logically and morally — and to vote for the candi
local.body:
This is the last weekend before the 2026 midterm elections. Most people have made up their minds already. Nevertheless, I'll use this platform to express a few opinions about some recent controversies in an effort to urge people to think critically -- logically and morally -- and to vote for the candidates who have the nation's best interest in their hearts and minds. While it's true that most people vote from their purses or wallets, I'd like to believe there is some idealism at play here. That there is an understanding of and belief in the Constitution, and a recognition of the importance of candidates’ character -- of their sense of decency and integrity.

There shouldn't be a debate over election security. Everyone agrees that citizens need to be legally registered in order to vote. Yet the controversy remains, despite overwhelming evidence that voter fraud is extremely rare. According to the American Bar Association, "Of the more than 25 million votes cast in six swing states in the 2020 election, an analysis by the Associated Press found fewer than 475 potential voter fraud cases, and even those cases were unconfirmed." Add to that the 59 local and federal courts who threw out alleged election fraud cases after the 2020 election.

Most importantly, we need to respect and appreciate those real people who work at the election sites. These are good, honest, everyday Americans performing a civic duty. They are democrats and republicans alike who, by and large, believe in free and fair elections. Hence, voter fraud should be a non-issue.

The controversy over the names of the candidates in the Alaskan Senate race is problematic. Allegedly, the campaign strategists for democrat candidate Mary Pelota concocted a scheme meant to confuse voters by bribing a man to enter the race who has a similar name as the republican candidate, incumbent Dan Sullivan. (This is a dirty trick used by both parties in the past.) Now Attorney General Todd Blanche, at the behest of his client/President, is proactively filing a lawsuit aiming to prevent the certification of the winner of that race if the incumbent Sullivan loses.

Obviously, the Democrats engaged slimy, dishonest and possibly illegal campaigning, and they should apologize to Alaska and the nation. However, the potential effects of such a ploy seem so inconsequential, and to litigate would be terribly insulting to the intelligence of the Alaskan voters. Are they really so stupid, so illiterate and brain-frozen that they can't read names? Don't know what incumbent means? That an S is no different than a J? Or that Daniel has six letters, Dan, three?

local.title: What kind of socialist are you?
local.summary: Anyone paying attention to state and federal politics has heard the word socialist ad nauseam ever since the 2024 elections. While on the campaign trail, President Donald Trump called Kamala Harris a socialist at every stop. Trump continues to call his political opponents socialists. During the 2026
local.body:
Anyone paying attention to state and federal politics has heard the word socialist ad nauseam ever since the 2024 elections. While on the campaign trail, President Donald Trump called Kamala Harris a socialist at every stop. Trump continues to call his political opponents socialists. During the 2026 election cycle, many Republican candidates have called their Democratic opponents socialists. In recent primaries, even Democrats have called fellow Democrats socialists and cautioned primary voters to beware.

As the phrase continues to be thrown around politically it may be helpful for individuals to examine the meaning of the word and to look at the platforms of politicians and the statements that they make to see if the candidates really are socialists. Understanding the meaning of the term may also help individuals determine if there is more to the word than just being a slur or an insult for a political opponent.

Socialism is defined as an economic and political system where the means of production — such as factories, land, machinery and natural resources — are owned or controlled collectively by the public, the community, or the state. A core characteristic of socialism is production for use where the economic focus is placed on meeting human needs such as food, housing, healthcare and education rather than generating private profit. There are different types and variations of socialism. While the United States operates fundamentally as a capitalist mixed economy, the government is filled with socialist programs that citizens make use of and benefit from every day.

Some examples of socialist programs in the U.S. government include public education, fire and police services, and our public works and infrastructure system. The roads that we drive on every day, the mail that we receive and the water and sewer systems that we use are all provided by socialism. Targeted safety net programs like Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP, Section 8 Housing and Social Security all operate under a model of collective security rather than private profit. While the U.S. military is not considered a completely socialist system, the U.S. military does operate using distinctly socialized principles. These socialist elements include state funding and ownership, universal socialized benefits for service members and their families and the lack of a free market profit motive. The U.S government doesn't profit off of our military. Defense contractors do.

local.body:
Thursday's free concert with the Army Field Band and Soldiers' Chorus was a homecoming for one member of the ensemble.

Maj. Philip Tappan, deputy commander of the United States Army Field Band, earned a master of music in Music Performance (Orchestral Conducting) from Fredonia in 2010 and a bachelor of music in Music Education in 2012.

Army Field Band's Concert Band and Soldiers' Chorus, the Army's premier touring ensembles, are comprised of a 60-piece concert band and a 24-voice chorus, featuring highly trained musicians from renowned institutions across the country.

While earning his master's degree at Fredonia, served as graduate assistant of Orchestras and Orchestral Conducting from 2008 to 2010. He returned to earn his bachelor's in Music Education and taught music in the Dunkirk City School District.

"I really enjoyed the teaching side of my graduate assistantship," Tappan said. "Teaching conducting to undergraduates was especially meaningful to me and remains one of the highlights of my time at Fredonia."

"The chamber orchestra performances were always exciting, especially when we performed early music in period style," Tappan said. "Those concerts stand out as some of my favorite musical experiences at Fredonia."

Tappan earned his Army commission in 2015 after graduating from Officer Candidate School at Fort Benning, Ga. His previous assignments include the Second Infantry Division Band and the United States Army Band "Pershing's Own," where he served as associate bandmaster; the First Cavalry Division Band as executive officer; the U.S. Army School of Music as commander and Director of Training; and the West Point Band at the United States Military Academy as deputy commander. He was deployed to Afghanistan twice, serving as officer in charge of the U.S. Forces - Afghanistan Band.

Tappan is also a composer, and his music has been performed at the Kennedy Center, the U.S. Embassy in Kabul, Afghanistan, and by professional and collegiate ensembles throughout the United States. His works span chamber, orchestral, and wind ensemble repertoire.

local.body:
On a cool, clear morning in October, members of the Bud 'n Bloom Garden Club enjoyed the autumn-colored trip to the lakeside home of Sharon and Ed Przybyciel.

The newly built home is nestled between the seasonal beauty of Lake Erie State Park, the gray, still waters of Lake Erie and a neighboring property set off by a recently built, short stone wall and a partially covered creek bed.

Following the curved driveway, the club members sighted huge pumpkins that decorated the walkway along with purple-green ajuga caressing the sidewalk, spikey bull weed and a large dark burgundy weeping Japanese maple. This split-leaf maple is also known as a Tamukeyama maple.

Corn stalks, huge stacked flat pumpkins, made into topiary towers of assorted colors and hand-cut wooden fall decor welcomed the visitors as they approached the home.

Inside, the home was festive with Halloween and autumn signs tucked around the kitchen, dining room and living room areas.

Worktables had been set up with crafting stations for each member containing canvas frames and easels, paint brushes, tacky glue and cups of water to clean the brushes.

In another area nearby, bags and trays held collections of beach glass, seashells, twigs, beach stones, assorted paints and markers for members’ selections. Lovely samples of finished samples were displayed.

As the crafters collected materials and started composing their creations, they enjoyed sharing ideas, the refreshments and the surrounding outdoor beauty.

What began a decade ago as an idea shared by the late Cristine Huff and fellow library staff has grown into a much-loved community tradition. From th
local.body:
For the past 10 years, the Anderson-Lee Library in Silver Creek has dedicated programming each November to celebrating Native American Heritage Month. What began a decade ago as an idea shared by the late Cristine Huff and fellow library staff has grown into a much-loved community tradition. From the beginning, one of the most important parts of the program has been the opportunity to build relationships and collaborate with members of the Seneca Nation.

This year's celebration will be especially meaningful as we gather not only to honor Native American heritage and culture, but also to remember and celebrate Huff and the lasting impact she had on our library and our community.

The special one-day event will take place on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Anderson-Lee Library, 43 Main St.

The day will begin at 11 a.m. with speakers and reflections, followed by a meal at noon featuring corn soup, frybread, and strawberry drink.

At 1 p.m., the library will dedicate this year's celebration in memory of Huff. Friends, family, library patrons, and members of the community will have an opportunity to gather, share stories, and remember her and the many programs she helped bring to life over the years.

For those who knew her, this event will be a chance to celebrate the enthusiasm, kindness, and dedication she brought to the library and to the community she cared so deeply about. For those who may not have had the opportunity to know her, it will be a chance to learn about the special role she played in creating a tradition that continues to bring people together.

Please join us as we celebrate Native American Heritage Month, honor her memory, and share in the community spirit that she helped make such an important part of this annual gathering.

local.title: Donald Trump looms over New York attorney general’s race
local.summary: Attorney General Letitia James, who has been a legal thorn in the president’s side, is seeking a third term.
local.body:
Few people have gotten under President Donald Trump’s skin quite the way New York Attorney General Letitia James has.

The Democratic attorney general has long been one of the president’s chief antagonists, suing the Republican’s administration more than 80 times since she took office in 2018 while becoming a frequent target of his ire on social media and at rallies.

Now, James has made her battles with Trump a central part of her campaign to win another four years in office.

“As I travel all throughout the state of New York and even the country, individuals thank me for standing up and protecting the interest of New Yorkers,” James said in an interview with Gothamist. “They thank me for recognizing that no one is above the law and that we do not bow to kings.”

But if she’s to win on Tuesday , she’ll have to overcome a challenge from Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor who has accused James of being “obsessed with national politics,” politicizing an office that should remain apolitical.

James, the former New York City public advocate who previously served as a city councilmember from Brooklyn, first rose to the attorney general’s office in the middle of Trump’s first term in 2018.

Since then, she has become a legal thorn in the president’s side.

Her lawsuits against the Trump administration — often leading a coalition of Democratic attorneys general from other states — have targeted the president’s actions on everything from immigration enforcement to Medicaid funding to housing grants.

local.summary: A Buffalo business owner is expanding - opening a new Main Street restaurant despite a longterm multimillion dollar construction project on his doorstep.
local.body: As a long-term construction project reshapes Buffalo's Main Street, some small businesses are struggling, but one owner is defying the trend by expanding.The $54 million federally funded project to allow cars to share Main Street with the train is set to continue until 2028. But signs of the strain on businesses are apparent, a bubble tea cafe closed down over the summer, along with nearby Greek restaurant Vasilis.Peter Flanagan owns lunch spot Pete's Place on the street. He tells me the construction has been a nuisance, but amidst the challenges he's decided to open a new restaurant at the former Vasilis location, next door to his current business.He's in the middle of renovating the space to become Sam's Benedict, a restaurant operated by his wife, Sam."The entire place is getting an overhaul, table chairs furniture, menu," Flanagan said.The business owner plans for the restaurant to be open for breakfast, lunch and dinner. He told me he's able to expand due to his wife's online catering business."Her reach has pulled the people in, and now our business is at capacity," Flanagan said.WATCH: Buffalo business owner expands with new restaurant despite ongoing Main Street construction woesFlanagan admitted he has some concerns about the length of the construction project but overall he's optimistic."I have high hopes for downtown. It's been dead since they first did this in the '70s when they put the rail in. Hopefully this fixes that mistake," Flanagan said. "Hopefully I can set an example for other businesses to come down here and be successful."Flanagan plans to open the new restaurant in January.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. local.body: A Newfane couple is becoming advocates to warn the public about the dangers of a synthetic form of Kratom after they say it claimed the life of their son.Jeff and Brenda Stunkel told me their 36-year-old son, Lucas, died by suicide earlier this month at their home. He had struggled with drug addiction but had been clean and sober for two-and-a-half years — until he took 7-OH, which he bought at a vape shop.The drug is a chemically altered form of Kratom, labeled "natural." It is illegal in 10 states already."I've read it's like 20 times more potent than morphine," Jeff Stunkel said. "It affects the same centers that your brain that opiates affect.”Brenda Stunkel pointed to the lack of oversight of the drug."There's no FDA regulation whatsoever, so they just do whatever they want, and they can package the pills themselves. The little packages come in with the five pills, those you can buy those packages over the internet with nothing in them, and they pop the pills in themselves," Brenda Stunkel said.The couple told me their son was at a rehab center in Niagara County trying to recover, but he called them begging for help."Please, please, please — I'm begging you to come get me," Lucas Stunkel said in a recorded phone message.Lucas came home, but shortly after — on Oct. 5 — he took his own life.Now, the couple are becoming advocates to educate the public about the dangers of this drug. entertainment.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Crashes Into Tokyo Film Festival With Stars Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe in Tow
entertainment.summary: Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel brought costumed fans, monster figurines and rapturous applause at two sold-out festival screenings ahead of its Nov. 3 Japanese release.
entertainment.body:
The King of Monsters finally stomped his way into Japan ’s largest celebration of cinema on Sunday as Takashi Yamazaki ’s wildly anticipated Godzilla Minus Zero played to a packed pair of screenings at the Tokyo International Film Festival.

The sold-out shows easily drew the liveliest crowds of this year’s Tokyo festival — the latest Toho -backed monster epic doesn’t open commercially in Japan until Nov. 3 — with numerous die-hard kaiju fans attending in costume or carrying their own Gojira figurines into the theater. Related Stories Music Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: "It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent" Movies 'Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting' Review: Whimsical Chinese Film Explores Myth and History Through a Series of Tasty Treats

Godzilla Minus Zero is playing as the “centerpiece film” of the Tokyo festival’s programming this year, and it undoubtedly brought a welcome jolt of energy to the event as it moves through its second half. When the credits rolled on the second screening inside Hulic Hall Tokyo, the crowd erupted into uncharacteristically rapturous applause, with the always respectful but typically subdued Japanese festivalgoers all smiles and excited chatter over favorite monster moments as they poured into the autumn evening in Tokyo’s Ginza district — where much of the carnage on screen takes place.

Godzilla Minus Zero is a direct follow-up to Godzilla Minus One (2023), which Yamazaki famously wrote, directed and VFX-supervised. The film was a smash with both critics and mainstream moviegoers, making history as the highest-grossing live-action Japanese film ever in North America ($57.1 million) and later becoming the first film in the multi-decade Godzilla franchise to take home an Oscar, winning the best visual effects award despite competing in the category against Hollywood tentpoles with vastly bigger budgets.

The sequel picks up in 1949, two years after the events of Minus One , as Japan struggles to rebuild from the devastation of war and Godzilla’s attack. The Shikishima family’s hard-won peace is threatened by a new calamity, with the film also bringing iconic franchise rival King Ghidorah, the three-headed kaiju, into Yamazaki’s postwar world.

Yamazaki’s return to the helm for the follow-up has lifted expectations across the globe — and the critical response so far, along with the enthusiastic reception at home in Tokyo on Sunday, suggests he delivered. Godzilla Minus Zero premiered in September at the New York Film Festival, where The Hollywood Reporter ’s chief critic David Rooney gave it a rave , calling the film a “radioactive blast” and “a crackling kaiju epic every bit as exciting as its predecessor.” The movie currently holds a score of 92 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 52 reviews.

For her first song, “ Hit the Wall ” from her third album Daughter from Hell , Abrams wore Claire Danes’ angel costume from the 1996 film and opened the performance from behind an aquarium, a nod to the movie’s fish-tank meeting scene. Her 2024 album The Secret of Us had peaked at No. 2.

Her highest-charting song to date remains “That’s So True,” the deluxe-edition track from The Secret of Us that reached No. 6 on the Hot 100 and became her first top 10 there.

Cast member Saidah Belo-Osagie played Minaj, bursting into the sketch near its end as James Austin Johnson’s Trump praised her loyalty to his movement. “Trump’s out here killing it,” Belo-Osagie’s Minaj declared, “and by it, I mean my career.” The sketch also cast her as Trump’s next choice for White House press secretary. Pumpkins, the oddball character he introduced on the show in 2016, backed by his dancing skeleton sidekicks Mikey Day and former cast member Bobby Moynihan, in what the sketch itself called the character’s third outing.

Before the bit could get going, Johnson’s Trump froze the scene and cut it short. “I’ll save you four minutes: he keeps popping up and confusing people on the ride. The end,” he told the audience, before comparing himself to Pumpkins: “We both appeared in 2016, we’re both very loud, very orange.” He went on to complain about Republican polling ahead of the midterms before Belo-Osagie’s Minaj made her entrance.

entertainment.title: ‘Green Room’ Director Recalls How Patrick Stewart “Saved” Movie From Being Scrapped
entertainment.summary: Ahead of a screening of the film on Friday, Jeremy Saulnier recounted how 'Green Room' was "close to shutting down" when the sci-fi icon, "out of the blue, expressed interest in the project."
entertainment.body:
Logo text Green Room director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to Patrick Stewart ahead of a Los Angeles screening of the film on Friday, recalling how the sci-fi icon “just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us.”

Celebrating the film’s 10th anniversary, Saulnier addressed the crowd and noted Stewart’s death at 86.

“Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” he said in a video posted on the Film Updates X account. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground , but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He every option to do otherwise.” Related Stories Movies Before 'Star Trek,' Patrick Stewart Proved His Sci-Fi Chops in 'Dune' Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist

The director remembered how production on Green Room was “at the point of no return, building sets, and under the gun without Darcy,” noting that the lead character of Darcy Banker had not yet been cast. However, that’s when the Star Trek star came in.

“We’re fucked, and we were close to shutting down. And Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” Saulnier said. “And in a whirlwind, about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage [thinking,] ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’ Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit.”

“We moved forward, and I thank him for just taking that leap and making Green Room a thing,” he added. “Patrick Stewart is why I still can make movies. He saved the day. Too good to be true.”

The Rebel Ridge director remembered Stewart as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, [who was a] very kind leader to our whole cast.” He also shared a story about how one day, the actor came to him and said he “wanted to add a little something” to a scene.

“I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, fuck!’ And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ I was like. ‘Permission granted, sir,’” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”

entertainment.title: Trump Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Story Dismissed by Judge
entertainment.summary: U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law.
entertainment.body:
Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump ’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein .

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal ’s investigative reporting. Related Stories TV Bill Maher Responds to Trump's 1,318-Word Social Rant: "He Went Off on Me Like Kelly Clarkson in a Toy Store" Music Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive)

When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.

Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists.

The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.

The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.

Douglas is 82, and Nicholson is 89. The two actors only professionally collaborated on 1975’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest , which Douglas produced and Nicholson starred in.

“That’s a good idea. I think I’ll have to think about that. I’m gonna think about that,” Trump responded , before suggesting that host Benny Johnson would also be “pretty good” for the position.

The exchange comes as Minaj has become increasingly involved in Trump’s political activities, including joining him at a Michigan rally ahead of this year’s midterm elections.

At the Oct. 25 rally in Port Huron, Minaj showed her support for Republican candidates Mike Rogers and John James. Trump also acknowledged Minaj’s presence at the rally, inviting her to stand before the crowd and drawing attention to her “beautiful a—” while addressing supporters.

entertainment.title: Deep Purple’s Ian Gillan Hospitalized Following Medical Emergency, Two Shows Postponed
entertainment.summary: The 81-year-old singer was scheduled to perform in Germany over the weekend.
entertainment.body:
Deep Purple frontman Ian Gillan has been hospitalized following a medical emergency, forcing the legendary British rock band to postpone two concerts in Germany.

In a statement shared on Instagram Saturday (Oct. 31), Deep Purple announced “with great disappointment” that its concert at QI Arena in Leipzig that evening, as well as its upcoming performance at Sporthalle Hamburg, had been postponed.

“This comes as a result of a medical emergency involving Ian Gillan, which has resulted in his current hospitalisation,” wrote the band, which also features guitarist Simon McBride, bassist Roger Glover, drummer Ian Paice and keyboardist Don Airey.

Deep Purple did not provide further details about Gillan’s condition or indicate when he might be released from the hospital.

“We understand that this announcement comes at short notice and share the disappointment of all our wonderful fans that we are unable to perform in Leipzig and Hamburg.”

The band added that it is working to find a “suitable time to reschedule” both concerts. Tickets purchased for the original dates will remain valid for the rescheduled performances.

Deep Purple has been on the road for its SPLAT! world tour since late summer, with additional dates scheduled across Europe, the United Kingdom, South America and Mexico through late December.

Gillan has served as Deep Purple’s lead vocalist during multiple stints, first joining the band in 1969. He is the voice behind some of the British rock group’s best-known hits such as “Smoke on the Water”and “Highway Star.”
